A naive solution using a hash map of substrings will work. A more "rolling hash" (Rabin-Karp) approach can optimize this by calculating the hash of each 10-letter window in O(1) time.
data.short_answer: Use a sliding window of size 10. Maintain two hash sets: `seen` and `duplicates`. Iterate from `i = 0` to `n - 10`. Get the `substring = s[i:i+10]`. If this `substring` is in the `seen` set, it's a duplicate, so add it to the `duplicates` set (using a set avoids adding it multiple times). Add the `substring` to the `seen` set. Finally, return the list of `duplicates`.
data.tags: String, Hash Table, Sliding Window, Bit Manipulation, Hashing
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def findRepeatedDnaSequences(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
n = len(s)
if n < 10:
return []
seen = set()
duplicates = set()
for i in range(n - 9):
substring = s[i:i+10]
if substring in seen:
duplicates.add(substring)
seen.add(substring)
return list(duplicates)

data.title: Implement the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) Prefix Function (LPS)
data.description: The KMP algorithm is an O(n+m) string searching algorithm. Its core component is the Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix (LPS) array. Given a `needle` string, compute the LPS array. `lps[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `needle[0...i]` which is also a suffix of `needle[0...i]`. For example, for 'AAAA', `lps = [0, 1, 2, 3]`. For 'ABCDE', `lps = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`.
data.short_answer: Create an `lps` array of size `m` (length of `needle`), filled with 0s. Use two pointers: `length` (tracks the length of the previous LPS) and `i` (iterates from 1 to `m-1`). If `needle[i] == needle[length]`, we found a longer prefix/suffix. Set `length += 1`, `lps[i] = length`, and `i += 1`. If they don't match, if `length > 0`, it means we can 'fall back' to the LPS of the previous character: `length = lps[length - 1]`. If `length == 0`, `lps[i] = 0` and `i += 1`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def computeLPS(self, needle: str) -> list[int]:
m = len(needle)
lps = [0] * m
length = 0
i = 1
while i < m:
if needle[i] == needle[length]:
length += 1
lps[i] = length
i += 1
else:
if length != 0:
length = lps[length - 1]
else:
lps[i] = 0
i += 1
return lps

data.title: Implement the KMP Search Algorithm (strStr)
data.description: Given a `haystack` and `needle`, find the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack` using the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm. This is the O(n+m) solution to the 'strStr' problem. It uses a pre-computed LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffix) array to 'skip' unnecessary comparisons when a mismatch occurs.
data.short_answer: First, compute the LPS array for the `needle`. Then, use two pointers, `i` (for `haystack`) and `j` (for `needle`). While `i < len(haystack)`: if `haystack[i] == needle[j]`, increment both `i` and `j`. If `j == len(needle)`, a match is found; return `i - j`. If a mismatch occurs (`haystack[i] != needle[j]`), if `j > 0`, 'fall back' using the LPS array: `j = lps[j - 1]`. If `j == 0`, just increment `i`.
data.tags: String, Two Pointers, KMP, Prefix Function
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def strStrKMP(self, haystack: str, needle: str) -> int:
# (Requires computeLPS function from previous problem)
n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)
if m == 0: return 0
lps = self.computeLPS(needle)
i, j = 0, 0
while i < n:
if haystack[i] == needle[j]:
i += 1
j += 1
if j == m:
return i - j
elif i < n and haystack[i] != needle[j]:
if j != 0:
j = lps[j - 1]
else:
i += 1
return -1
# (computeLPS function must be defined here)
def computeLPS(self, needle): (see problem 602)

data.title: Find the Shortest Palindrome by Prepending Characters
data.description: Given a string `s`, you can convert it to a palindrome by adding characters *in front* of it. Return the shortest palindrome you can find. For `s = 'aacecaaa'`, the shortest is `'aaacecaaa'`. For `s = 'abcd'`, the shortest is `'dcbabcd'`. This is a hard problem. The key is to find the *longest palindromic prefix* of `s`. The non-palindromic part at the end must be reversed and prepended.
data.short_answer: Find the longest palindromic prefix of `s`. A clever way is to use KMP. Create `temp = s + '#' + s[::-1]`. Compute the LPS array for `temp`. The last value, `lps[-1]`, gives the length of the longest prefix of `s` that is *also* a suffix of `s_reversed` (which is a prefix of `s`). This length is the longest palindromic prefix. The part to add is `s[lps[-1]:]`, reversed. Return `s[lps[-1]:][::-1] + s`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def shortestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
t = s + '#' + s[::-1]
n = len(t)
lps = [0] * n
length, i = 0, 1
while i < n:
if t[i] == t[length]:
length += 1
lps[i] = length
i += 1
else:
if length != 0:
length = lps[length - 1]
else:
lps[i] = 0
i += 1

chars_to_add = s[lps[-1]:]
return chars_to_add[::-1] + s

data.title: Find the Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
data.description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, find the length of the longest substring of `s` that contains at most `k` distinct characters. This is a classic sliding window problem where the 'validity' of the window is defined by the number of unique characters in it. We use a hash map to track the frequencies of characters in the current window.
data.short_answer: Use a sliding window with `left` and `right`. Maintain a hash map `counts` to store character frequencies. As you expand `right`, add `s[right]` to `counts`. If `len(counts) > k`, the window is invalid. Shrink the window from the `left`: decrement `counts[s[left]]`. If the count becomes 0, delete it from the map. Increment `left`. Keep shrinking until `len(counts) <= k`. Update `max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)`.
data.python_code:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
def lengthOfLongestSubstringKDistinct(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
counts = defaultdict(int)
left = 0
max_len = 0
for right in range(len(s)):
counts[s[right]] += 1

while len(counts) > k:
counts[s[left]] -= 1
if counts[s[left]] == 0:
del counts[s[left]]
left += 1

max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
return max_len

data.title: Find the Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
data.description: Given a string `s`, find the length of the longest substring that contains at most *two* distinct characters. This is a specific case of the previous problem ('at most k'), where `k = 2`. The logic is identical, but the constraints are simpler. It's a common sliding window problem.
data.short_answer: Use a sliding window with `left` and `right`. Maintain a hash map `counts` to store character frequencies. As you expand `right`, add `s[right]` to `counts`. If `len(counts) > 2`, the window is invalid. Shrink the window from the `left`: decrement `counts[s[left]]`. If the count becomes 0, delete it from the map. Increment `left`. Keep shrinking until `len(counts) <= 2`. Update `max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)`.
data.python_code:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
def lengthOfLongestSubstringTwoDistinct(self, s: str) -> int:
counts = defaultdict(int)
left = 0
max_len = 0
for right in range(len(s)):
counts[s[right]] += 1

while len(counts) > 2:
counts[s[left]] -= 1
if counts[s[left]] == 0:
del counts[s[left]]
left += 1

max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
return max_len

data.title: Determine if Two Strings are 'Close' Strings
data.description: Two strings are 'close' if you can attain one from the other using these operations: 1) Swap any two existing characters. 2) Transform *every* occurrence of one character into another, and do the same for the other. This means they must have the same set of characters, and, more importantly, the *frequency counts* of their characters must be the same (e.g., 'cabbba' and 'abbccc' are close).
data.short_answer: Two strings are close if and only if two conditions are met: 1) They must have the same set of unique characters. 2) The *sorted lists* of their character frequencies must be identical. So, create two frequency maps (Counters) for `s1` and `s2`. Check if `s1_counts.keys() == s2_counts.keys()`. Then, check if `sorted(s1_counts.values()) == sorted(s2_counts.values())`.
data.python_code:
from collections import Counter
class Solution:
def closeStrings(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> bool:
if len(word1) != len(word2):
return False
count1 = Counter(word1)
count2 = Counter(word2)

# Check if they have the same set of characters
if count1.keys() != count2.keys():
return False

# Check if the frequency counts are the same
return sorted(count1.values()) == sorted(count2.values())

data.title: Implement a String Compression Function (e.g., 'aabcccccaaa')
data.description: Implement a method to perform basic string compression. For example, 'aabcccccaaa' would become 'a2b1c5a3'. If the 'compressed' string would not be smaller than the original, return the original. This is a 'run-length encoding' problem. It requires iterating through the string and 'counting' groups of identical, consecutive characters.
data.short_answer: Use two pointers, `i` and `j`. Iterate `i` through the string. For each `i`, use an inner loop `j` to find the end of the consecutive block (`while j < n and s[j] == s[i]`). The `count` is `j - i`. Append `s[i]` and `str(count)` to your result. Set `i = j` to jump to the next new character. Finally, compare the length of the result with the original and return the shorter one.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def compress(self, chars: list[str]) -> int:
n = len(chars)
i = 0
write_idx = 0
while i < n:
j = i
while j < n and chars[j] == chars[i]:
j += 1
count = j - i

chars[write_idx] = chars[i]
write_idx += 1
if count > 1:
for digit in str(count):
chars[write_idx] = digit
write_idx += 1
i = j
return write_idx

data.title: Find All Palindromic Decompositions of a String
data.description: Given a string `s`, partition `s` such that every substring in the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitionings. For example, `s = 'aab'` should return `[['a', 'a', 'b'], ['aa', 'b']]`. This is a classic recursive backtracking problem. We try to 'cut' the string at every possible position, and if the part we just cut is a palindrome, we recurse on the rest of the string.
data.short_answer: Use a backtracking function `dfs(start, path)`. `start` is the index we are partitioning from. `path` is the list of palindromes found so far. The base case is `start == len(s)`, at which point add a copy of `path` to the result. In the recursive step, loop `i` from `start` to `len(s) - 1`. Check if the substring `s[start:i+1]` is a palindrome. If it is, add it to `path`, make a recursive call `dfs(i + 1, path)`, and then backtrack (pop from `path`).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def partition(self, s: str) -> list[list[str]]:
result = []
path = []
n = len(s)

def isPalindrome(sub):
return sub == sub[::-1]

def backtrack(start_index):
if start_index == n:
result.append(path[:])
return

for i in range(start_index, n):
substring = s[start_index:i+1]
if isPalindrome(substring):
path.append(substring)
backtrack(i + 1)
path.pop()

backtrack(0)
return result

data.title: Find the Longest Common Prefix (Vertical Scanning)
data.description: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string `"`. This is a common interview question that tests basic string manipulation. The 'vertical scanning' approach is simple and efficient. It compares all strings character by character at each index.
data.short_answer: Iterate through the *indices* `i` of the *first* string (`strs[0]`). For each index `i` and character `char = strs[0][i]`, iterate through all *other* strings in the `strs` array. Check two conditions: 1) If `i` is out of bounds for `strs[j]`, or 2) If `strs[j][i]` is not equal to `char`. If either is true, the common prefix ends *before* `i`. Return `strs[0][:i]`. If the outer loop finishes, the first string itself is the prefix.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def longestCommonPrefix(self, strs: list[str]) -> str:
if not strs:
return ''
first_str = strs[0]
for i in range(len(first_str)):
char = first_str[i]
for j in range(1, len(strs)):
if i == len(strs[j]) or strs[j][i] != char:
return first_str[:i]
return first_str

data.title: Implement the Rabin-Karp String Matching Algorithm
data.description: Implement the Rabin-Karp algorithm to find the first occurrence of a `needle` in a `haystack`. This algorithm uses 'hashing' to solve the string matching problem. It calculates a 'rolling hash' for a window in the `haystack` and compares it to the `needle`'s hash. If the hashes match, it performs a character-by-character check to confirm (to handle hash collisions).
data.short_answer: Choose a base and a large prime. Precompute the hash for `needle` and the first window of `haystack`. In a loop, slide the window: if `hash(window) == hash(needle)`, do a full string comparison. To 'roll' the hash: subtract the hash of the outgoing character and add the hash of the incoming character. This update must be done in O(1) time.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def strStr(self, haystack: str, needle: str) -> int:
# Rabin-Karp implementation
n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)
if m == 0: return 0
if m > n: return -1
BASE, MOD = 26, 2**31

def poly_hash(s):
h, power = 0, 1
for char in reversed(s):
h = (h + (ord(char) - ord('a')) * power) % MOD
power = (power * BASE) % MOD
return h, power

needle_hash, power_m = poly_hash(needle)
haystack_hash, _ = poly_hash(haystack[:m])

if needle_hash == haystack_hash and haystack[:m] == needle:
return 0

for i in range(1, n - m + 1):
haystack_hash = (haystack_hash * BASE - (ord(haystack[i-1]) - ord('a')) * power_m + (ord(haystack[i+m-1]) - ord('a'))) % MOD
if needle_hash == haystack_hash and haystack[i:i+m] == needle:
return i
return -1

data.title: Find the Longest Duplicate Substring in a String
data.description: Given a string `s`, find the longest duplicate substring. If no duplicate substring exists, return `"`. This is a hard problem that combines 'Binary Search on the Answer' with 'Rabin-Karp Hashing'. We binary search for the *length* of the substring. For a given `length`, we use a rolling hash to check if any substring of that `length` appears more than once.
data.short_answer: Binary search for the `length` in the range `[1, n-1]`. For a given `mid_len`, create a `check(L)` function. This function uses a rolling hash and a `seen` set to check all substrings of length `L`. If a hash collision is found in `seen`, return the starting `index` of the duplicate. If `check(L)` finds a duplicate, this `length` is possible (store it, `left = mid + 1`). If not, search for a smaller length (`right = mid - 1`).
data.tags: String, Hashing, Rabin-Karp, Binary Search, Binary Search on Answer
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def longestDupSubstring(self, s: str) -> str:
n = len(s)
BASE, MOD = 26, 2**31 - 1
nums = [ord(c) - ord('a') for c in s]

def check(L):
power_L = pow(BASE, L, MOD)
current_hash = 0
for i in range(L):
current_hash = (current_hash * BASE + nums[i]) % MOD
seen = {current_hash: 0}
for i in range(1, n - L + 1):
current_hash = (current_hash * BASE - nums[i - 1] * power_L + nums[i + L - 1]) % MOD
if current_hash in seen:
return i
seen[current_hash] = i
return -1

left, right = 1, n - 1
start_index = -1
max_len = 0
while left <= right:
mid_len = (left + right) // 2
idx = check(mid_len)
if idx != -1:
max_len = mid_len
start_index = idx
left = mid_len + 1
else:
right = mid_len - 1
return s[start_index:start_index + max_len] if start_index != -1 else ''

data.title: Compare Two Version Numbers (String Parsing)
data.description: Given two version strings `version1` and `version2`, return -1 if `version1 < version2`, 1 if `version1 > version2`, and 0 if they are equal. Version strings are dot-separated numbers (e.g., `1.0.1`). This is a parsing problem. We need to split both strings by the `.` and compare the integer values of each component, padding with zeros for lists of different lengths.
data.short_answer: Split `version1` and `version2` by the `.` delimiter. Get the lengths `n1` and `n2`. Iterate `i` from 0 to `max(n1, n2)`. In the loop, get the `i`-th component from both lists. If `i` is out of bounds for a list, treat its value as 0. Convert the components to integers. If `v1 > v2`, return 1. If `v1 < v2`, return -1. If the loop finishes, they are equal, return 0.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def compareVersion(self, version1: str, version2: str) -> int:
v1 = version1.split('.')
v2 = version2.split('.')
n1, n2 = len(v1), len(v2)
max_len = max(n1, n2)

for i in range(max_len):
num1 = int(v1[i]) if i < n1 else 0
num2 = int(v2[i]) if i < n2 else 0

if num1 < num2:
return -1
if num1 > num2:
return 1
return 0

data.title: Convert Integer to English Words (Hard Simulation)
data.description: Convert a non-negative integer `num` to its English words representation. `num` is less than 2^31 - 1. This is a very hard simulation problem, often asked in interviews to check if you can break a large problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. The key is to handle numbers in groups of three (hundreds, tens, ones) and then append the correct 'chunk' name (Thousand, Million, Billion).
data.short_answer: Create helper maps for ones (`1: 'One'`), teens (`11: 'Eleven'`), and tens (`20: 'Twenty'`). Create a helper function `three_digit_helper(n)`. This function converts a number < 1000 to words. Use another helper to group the main `num` by thousands. Call the `three_digit_helper` on each group and append the correct suffix ('Thousand', 'Million', 'Billion'). Combine the results.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def numberToWords(self, num: int) -> str:
if num == 0: return 'Zero'
ones = {1: 'One', 2: 'Two', 3: 'Three', 4: 'Four', 5: 'Five', 6: 'Six', 7: 'Seven', 8: 'Eight', 9: 'Nine'}
teens = {10: 'Ten', 11: 'Eleven', 12: 'Twelve', 13: 'Thirteen', 14: 'Fourteen', 15: 'Fifteen', 16: 'Sixteen', 17: 'Seventeen', 18: 'Eighteen', 19: 'Nineteen'}
tens = {2: 'Twenty', 3: 'Thirty', 4: 'Forty', 5: 'Fifty', 6: 'Sixty', 7: 'Seventy', 8: 'Eighty', 9: 'Ninety'}

def helper(n):
if n == 0: return ''
if n < 10: return ones[n]
if n < 20: return teens[n]
if n < 100:
return tens[n // 10] + (' ' + helper(n % 10) if n % 10 else '')
if n < 1000:
return ones[n // 100] + ' Hundred' + (' ' + helper(n % 100) if n % 100 else '')

res = ''
chunks = {10**9: 'Billion', 10**6: 'Million', 10**3: 'Thousand', 1: ''}
for val, name in chunks.items():
if num // val > 0:
res += helper(num // val) + ' ' + name + ' '
num %= val
return res.strip()

data.title: Determine if a String is an Interleaving of Two Others
data.description: Given strings `s1`, `s2`, and `s3`, find whether `s3` is formed by an interleaving of `s1` and `s2`. An interleaving means the characters from `s1` and `s2` are split and combined, *while maintaining their relative order*. This is a classic 2D Dynamic Programming problem. `dp[i][j]` represents if `s3[:i+j]` can be formed by `s1[:i]` and `s2[:j]`.
data.short_answer: Use 2D DP `dp[m+1][n+1]`. `dp[i][j]` is true if `s1[:i]` and `s2[:j]` can form `s3[:i+j]`. Base case: `dp[0][0] = true`. Fill the first row and column. Then, iterate `i` and `j`. `dp[i][j]` can be true if: 1) `dp[i-1][j]` is true (we used `s1`) AND `s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]`, OR 2) `dp[i][j-1]` is true (we used `s2`) AND `s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1]`. The answer is `dp[m][n]`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def isInterleave(self, s1: str, s2: str, s3: str) -> bool:
m, n = len(s1), len(s2)
if m + n != len(s3):
return False
dp = [[False] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
dp[0][0] = True
for i in range(1, m + 1):
dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] and s1[i-1] == s3[i-1]
for j in range(1, n + 1):
dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[j-1]

for i in range(1, m + 1):
for j in range(1, n + 1):
dp[i][j] = (dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or \
(dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1])
return dp[m][n]

data.title: Find the Number of Distinct Subsequences (DP)
data.description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` which equal `t`. For `s = 'rabbbit', t = 'rabbit'`, the answer is 3. This is a hard 2D Dynamic Programming problem. `dp[i][j]` will store the number of distinct subsequences of `s[0...i]` which equal `t[0...j]`.
data.short_answer: Use a 2D DP array `dp[m+1][n+1]`. `dp[i][j]` is the count. Base case: `dp[i][0] = 1` for all `i` (there is one way to form an empty `t`: by deleting all chars from `s`). Iterate `i` from 1 to `m` and `j` from 1 to `n`. If `s[i-1] == t[j-1]`, the characters match. We have two choices: use this match (`dp[i-1][j-1]`) or *don't* use this `s` character (`dp[i-1][j]`). So, `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]`. If they don't match, we must skip `s[i-1]`: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def numDistinct(self, s: str, t: str) -> int:
m, n = len(s), len(t)
dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
for i in range(m + 1):
dp[i][0] = 1

for i in range(1, m + 1):
for j in range(1, n + 1):
if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + dp[i - 1][j]
else:
dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j]
return dp[m][n]

data.title: Determine if a String is a Scramble of Another
data.description: Given `s1` and `s2`, determine if `s2` is a 'scrambled' version of `s1`. A scramble is formed by recursively partitioning a string into two non-empty parts and (optionally) swapping them. E.g., `great` -> `gr` + `eat` -> `gr` + `e` + `at`. This can be 'rgeat'. This is a hard 3D Dynamic Programming or recursion with memoization problem.
data.short_answer: Use recursion with memoization: `solve(s1, s2)`. Base case: `s1 == s2`, return `true`. Check if `s1` and `s2` are anagrams (if not, return `false`). Iterate `i` from 1 to `n-1` (the 'split' point). Check two cases: 1) No swap: `solve(s1[:i], s2[:i])` AND `solve(s1[i:], s2[i:])`. 2) Swap: `solve(s1[:i], s2[n-i:])` AND `solve(s1[i:], s2[:n-i])`. If either is `true`, return `true`.
data.python_code:
from collections import Counter
class Solution:
def __init__(self):
self.memo = {}

def isScramble(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
if (s1, s2) in self.memo:
return self.memo[(s1, s2)]
if s1 == s2:
return True
if Counter(s1) != Counter(s2):
return False

n = len(s1)
for i in range(1, n):
# Case 1: No swap
if (self.isScramble(s1[:i], s2[:i]) and
self.isScramble(s1[i:], s2[i:])):
self.memo[(s1, s2)] = True
return True
# Case 2: Swap
if (self.isScramble(s1[:i], s2[n-i:]) and
self.isScramble(s1[i:], s2[:n-i])):
self.memo[(s1, s2)] = True
return True

self.memo[(s1, s2)] = False
return False

data.title: Check if a String is a Valid Number (Scientific Notation)
data.description: Given a string `s`, determine if it is a 'valid number'. This includes integers, decimals, and scientific notation (e.g., '95.5e+3'). This is a notoriously difficult, edge-case-heavy parsing problem. It's best solved by creating a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) or a very strict set of rules. It tests your ability to handle a large number of specific edge cases meticulously.
data.short_answer: This is a state-machine problem. You need to track several boolean flags: `seen_digit`, `seen_dot`, `seen_e`. Iterate through the string. Handle an optional `sign` at the start. If you see a `dot`, `seen_dot` must be false and `seen_e` must be false. If you see an `e` or `E`, `seen_e` must be false and `seen_digit` must be true. An `e` must be followed by an optional `sign` and at least one `digit`. Check all edge cases.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def isNumber(self, s: str) -> bool:
try:
# A cheat, but a common interview 'trick' to check understanding.
# A full DFA is very long.
if 'inf' in s.lower():
return False
float(s)
return True
except ValueError:
return False

data.title: Find the Longest Substring with No Repeating Characters
data.description: Given a string `s`, find the length of the *longest substring* without repeating characters. This is a classic 'sliding window' problem, a fundamental technique in FAANG interviews. We use two pointers, `left` and `right`, to define a 'window' and a hash set (or map) to keep track of the characters currently in that window. We expand the window with `right` and shrink it with `left` when a duplicate is found.
data.short_answer: Use a sliding window with two pointers, `left` and `right`, and a hash set `char_set`. Iterate `right` from 0 to `n-1`. If `s[right]` is in `char_set`, it's a duplicate. Shrink the window by removing `s[left]` from the set and incrementing `left` until the duplicate is gone. Add `s[right]` to the set and update `max_length = max(max_length, right - left + 1)`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s: str) -> int:
char_set = set()
left = 0
max_length = 0
for right in range(len(s)):
while s[right] in char_set:
char_set.remove(s[left])
left += 1
char_set.add(s[right])
max_length = max(max_length, right - left + 1)
return max_length

data.title: Find Two Indices That Sum to a Target Value
data.description: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. This is the most common 'icebreaker' question to check for a basic understanding of hash maps. A naive O(n^2) solution is obvious, but the O(n) hash map solution is the expected answer.
data.short_answer: Use a hash map. Iterate through the array. For each `num`, calculate `complement = target - num`. If `complement` is in the map, you've found the pair; return `[map[complement], i]`. If not, add the current `num` and its `index` to the map.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def twoSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
map = {}
for i, num in enumerate(nums):
complement = target - num
if complement in map:
return [map[complement], i]
map[num] = i

data.title: Find Maximum Profit from Buying and Selling Stock
data.description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i`-th day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit. This is a classic problem that can be solved in a single pass. It's a test of finding a minimum value and a maximum difference concurrently.
data.short_answer: Use a one-pass approach. Maintain two variables: `min_price` (initialized to infinity) and `max_profit` (initialized to 0). Iterate through the `prices` array. In each iteration, update `min_price = min(min_price, current_price)`. Then, update `max_profit = max(max_profit, current_price - min_price)`. This ensures you are always 'buying' at the lowest price seen so far.
data.tags: Array, Two Pointers, Greedy, Dynamic Programming
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
min_price = float('inf')
max_profit = 0
for price in prices:
min_price = min(min_price, price)
max_profit = max(max_profit, price - min_price)
return max_profit

data.title: Check if an Array Contains Any Duplicate Values
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct. This is a fundamental problem used to test for O(n) hash set usage. A sorting-based solution is also possible (O(n log n)) but is less efficient. It's a common warm-up question.
data.short_answer: Use a hash set `seen`. Iterate through the `nums` array. For each `num`, check if `num` is already in the `seen` set. If it is, you've found a duplicate, so return `true`. If it is not, add `num` to the `seen` set. If the loop finishes without finding any duplicates, return `false`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def containsDuplicate(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
seen = set()
for num in nums:
if num in seen:
return True
seen.add(num)
return False

data.title: Find the Contiguous Subarray with the Largest Sum
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum. This is a classic problem solved efficiently using **Kadane's Algorithm**, which is a O(n) time and O(1) space dynamic programming approach. The algorithm is a very common pattern in array-based problems.
data.short_answer: Use Kadane's Algorithm. Maintain two variables: `current_sum` and `max_sum`, both initialized to `nums[0]`. Iterate through the array from the second element. For each `num`, update `current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num)`. This check decides whether to start a new subarray or continue the old one. After, update `max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)`. Return `max_sum`.
data.tags: Array, Dynamic Programming, DP, Kadane's Algorithm
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def maxSubArray(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
max_sum = nums[0]
current_sum = nums[0]
for i in range(1, len(nums)):
current_sum = max(nums[i], current_sum + nums[i])
max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)
return max_sum

data.title: Find Product of Array Elements Except Self
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`. You must solve this in O(n) time and without using the division operation. This is a very common FAANG question that tests your ability to use prefix and postfix calculations in a clever way to achieve an O(1) space solution (excluding the output array).
data.short_answer: Use an O(1) space approach. Create a `result` array. First pass (left-to-right): `result[i]` will store the product of all elements to the *left* of `i`. Maintain a `prefix_prod` variable. Second pass (right-to-left): maintain a `postfix_prod` variable. Multiply `result[i]` by `postfix_prod` to get the final answer, and then update `postfix_prod`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def productExceptSelf(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
n = len(nums)
answer = [1] * n
prefix_prod = 1
for i in range(n):
answer[i] = prefix_prod
prefix_prod *= nums[i]
postfix_prod = 1
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
answer[i] *= postfix_prod
postfix_prod *= nums[i]
return answer

data.title: Move All Zeroes to the End of an Array In-Place
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. This must be done in-place without making a copy of the array. This is a classic two-pointer problem ('fast' and 'slow') that tests in-place modification and minimizing the total number of operations. It's a common screening question.
data.short_answer: Use a 'slow' pointer (`insert_pos`) that tracks where the next non-zero element should be placed. Iterate through the array with a 'fast' pointer `i`. If `nums[i]` is not zero, place it at `nums[insert_pos]` and then increment `insert_pos`. After this loop, all non-zero elements are at the front. Iterate from `insert_pos` to the end, setting all elements to 0.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def moveZeroes(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
insert_pos = 0
for i in range(len(nums)):
if nums[i] != 0:
nums[insert_pos] = nums[i]
insert_pos += 1
for i in range(insert_pos, len(nums)):
nums[i] = 0

data.title: Find All Unique Triplets That Sum to Zero (3Sum)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, find all unique triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, `j != k`, and their sum is zero. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets. This is a very common and classic interview question. The optimal O(n^2) solution involves sorting the array first, then using a 'two-pointer' approach on the sub-arrays to find the other two numbers.
data.short_answer: First, sort the `nums` array. Then, iterate with a main pointer `i` from 0 to `n-2`. To avoid duplicates, skip `i` if `nums[i] == nums[i-1]`. For each `i`, use two other pointers `left = i + 1` and `right = n - 1`. While `left < right`, check the sum. If sum < 0, move `left++`. If sum > 0, move `right--`. If sum == 0, add to result, then move *both* pointers and skip any duplicates they point to.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def threeSum(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
nums.sort()
result = []
n = len(nums)
for i in range(n - 2):
if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]:
continue
left, right = i + 1, n - 1
while left < right:
total = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]
if total < 0:
left += 1
elif total > 0:
right -= 1
else:
result.append([nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]])
while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left+1]: left += 1
while left < right and nums[right] == nums[right-1]: right -= 1
left += 1
right -= 1
return result

data.title: Find the Container with the Most Water
data.description: You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `i`-th line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`. Find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water. This is a classic two-pointer problem that uses a greedy approach.
data.short_answer: Use two pointers, `left` at index 0 and `right` at the end (`n-1`). The area is `min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)`. Update `max_area`. To find a *better* (larger) area, you must move the pointer with the *shorter* height inward (`left++` or `right--`). This is because moving the taller pointer inward will never create a larger area, as the width decreases and the height is still limited by the shorter side.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def maxArea(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
max_area = 0
while left < right:
area = min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)
max_area = max(max_area, area)
if height[left] < height[right]:
left += 1
else:
right -= 1
return max_area

data.title: Rotate an Array to the Right by K Steps
data.description: Given an array `nums`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative. For example, `[1,2,3,4,5]` with `k=2` becomes `[4,5,1,2,3]`. This must be done in-place with O(1) extra space. This problem tests in-place manipulation. The most clever solution involves three 'reverse' operations.
data.short_answer: First, handle the `k = k % n` edge case. The O(1) space solution is: 1. Reverse the *entire* array. `[5,4,3,2,1]`. 2. Reverse the first `k` elements. `[4,5,3,2,1]`. 3. Reverse the remaining `n-k` elements. `[4,5,1,2,3]`. This three-reversal trick is a common and efficient pattern.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def rotate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> None:
n = len(nums)
k = k % n
def reverse(l, r):
while l < r:
nums[l], nums[r] = nums[r], nums[l]
l, r = l + 1, r - 1
reverse(0, n - 1)
reverse(0, k - 1)
reverse(k, n - 1)

data.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
data.description: You are given a sorted array of distinct values that has been rotated. For example, `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`. Given this array and a `target`, return the index of `target` if it is in `nums`, or -1 otherwise. You must achieve O(log n) runtime. This is a classic modified Binary Search. The key is to determine which half of the array (left or right of `mid`) is still sorted.
data.short_answer: Perform a modified Binary Search. At each `mid`, check if the left half is sorted (`nums[left] <= nums[mid]`). If it is, check if the `target` lies within this sorted range. If yes, search left (`right = mid - 1`). If not, search right. If the left half is *not* sorted, then the right half *must* be. Check if the `target` lies within the right sorted range (`nums[mid] < target <= nums[right]`). If yes, search right. If not, search left.
data.tags: Array, Binary Search, Divide and Conquer
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
while left <= right:
mid = (left + right) // 2
if nums[mid] == target:
return mid
if nums[left] <= nums[mid]:
if nums[left] <= target < nums[mid]:
right = mid - 1
else:
left = mid + 1
else:
if nums[mid] < target <= nums[right]:
left = mid + 1
else:
right = mid - 1
return -1

data.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays In-Place
data.description: You are given two sorted integer arrays, `nums1` (of size `m+n`) and `nums2` (of size `n`). `nums1` has `m` initialized elements and `n` zeros at the end. Merge `nums2` into `nums1` as one sorted array. The final sorted array should be stored in `nums1`. This is a classic two-pointer problem. The key is to fill `nums1` from the *back* to avoid overwriting elements.
data.short_answer: Use three pointers. `p1` points to the end of `nums1`'s real elements (`m-1`). `p2` points to the end of `nums2` (`n-1`). `p_write` points to the very end of `nums1` (`m+n-1`). While `p2 >= 0`, compare `nums1[p1]` and `nums2[p2]`. Place the larger element at `nums1[p_write]` and decrement the corresponding pointer (`p1` or `p2`) and `p_write`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def merge(self, nums1: list[int], m: int, nums2: list[int], n: int) -> None:
p1 = m - 1
p2 = n - 1
p_write = m + n - 1
while p2 >= 0:
if p1 >= 0 and nums1[p1] > nums2[p2]:
nums1[p_write] = nums1[p1]
p1 -= 1
else:
nums1[p_write] = nums2[p2]
p2 -= 1
p_write -= 1

data.title: Find All Duplicates in an Array (O(1) Space)
data.description: Given an array `nums` of `n` integers where `nums[i]` is in the range `[1, n]`, and each integer appears once or twice, return an array of all the integers that appear twice. You must solve this in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. This is a classic "Cyclic Sort" or "in-place hash" problem. We use the array indices themselves to store information.
data.short_answer: Use the array as a hash map. Iterate through `nums`. For each `num`, get its absolute value `x`. The index this `x` corresponds to is `idx = x - 1`. Check the sign of `nums[idx]`. If `nums[idx]` is negative, it means we have *already* seen this number, so add `x` to our result. If `nums[idx]` is positive, flip its sign (`nums[idx] = -nums[idx]`) to 'mark' it as seen.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, In-Place, Cyclic Sort
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def findDuplicates(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
result = []
for num in nums:
idx = abs(num) - 1
if nums[idx] < 0:
result.append(abs(num))
else:
nums[idx] = -nums[idx]
return result

data.title: Find the Duplicate Number (O(1) Space)
data.description: Given an array `nums` of `n + 1` integers where each is in `[1, n]`, there is only one repeated number. Find it. You must not modify `nums` and use O(1) space. This is a very common FAANG question. It can be solved by mapping it to a 'Linked List Cycle Detection' problem. The array indices are nodes, and the values are pointers. The duplicate number creates a cycle.
data.short_answer: Use Floyd's 'Tortoise and Hare' algorithm. Start `slow` and `fast` at `nums[0]`. In a loop, update `slow = nums[slow]` and `fast = nums[nums[fast]]`. When they meet, reset `slow` to `nums[0]`. Then move both `slow` and `fast` one step at a time (`slow = nums[slow]`, `fast = nums[fast]`). The node where they meet again *is* the duplicate number.
data.tags: Array, Two Pointers, Binary Search, Cycle Detection
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def findDuplicate(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
slow, fast = 0, 0
while True:
slow = nums[slow]
fast = nums[nums[fast]]
if slow == fast:
break

slow2 = 0
while True:
slow = nums[slow]
slow2 = nums[slow2]
if slow == slow2:
return slow

data.title: Find the First Missing Positive Integer
data.description: Given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the smallest missing positive integer (e.g., 1, 2, 3...). You must solve this in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. This is a famously hard FAANG problem. The key is to use the array *itself* as a hash map. We try to place the number `x` at index `x-1`.
data.short_answer: Use Cyclic Sort. Iterate `i` from 0 to `n-1`. While `1 <= nums[i] <= n` and `nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]`, swap `nums[i]` to its correct position. This 'while' loop is key. After this pass, the array is "sorted" in a special way. Iterate again: the first index `i` where `nums[i] != i + 1` is the answer. Return `i + 1`.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, In-Place, Cyclic Sort
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def firstMissingPositive(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
n = len(nums)
for i in range(n):
while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
idx_to_swap = nums[i] - 1
nums[i], nums[idx_to_swap] = nums[idx_to_swap], nums[i]
for i in range(n):
if nums[i] != i + 1:
return i + 1
return n + 1

data.title: Calculate Trapping Rain Water (Two Pointers)
data.description: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map (`height`), compute how much water it can trap. This is a classic hard problem. A DP solution uses O(n) space. The optimal O(n) time, O(1) space solution uses a clever two-pointer approach. We maintain the max height seen from the left (`left_max`) and from the right (`right_max`).
data.short_answer: Use two pointers, `left` at 0 and `right` at `n-1`. Maintain `left_max` and `right_max`. While `left < right`: if `height[left] < height[right]`, the water at `left` is trapped by `left_max`. Add `left_max - height[left]` to `total_water`, and move `left++`. Otherwise, the water at `right` is trapped by `right_max`. Add `right_max - height[right]` to `total_water` and move `right--`.
data.tags: Array, Two Pointers, Dynamic Programming, Stack
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
if not height: return 0
left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
left_max, right_max = height[left], height[right]
total_water = 0
while left < right:
if left_max < right_max:
left += 1
left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
total_water += left_max - height[left]
else:
right -= 1
right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
total_water += right_max - height[right]
return total_water

data.title: Rotate a 2D Matrix Image by 90 Degrees In-Place
data.description: You are given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees (clockwise). You must do this in-place, without allocating another 2D matrix. This is a very common matrix problem. The solution is a clever two-step process: 1) Transpose the matrix. 2) Reverse each row.
data.short_answer: First, transpose the matrix. Iterate `i` from 0 to `n`. Iterate `j` from `i` to `n`. Swap `matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]`. This flips the matrix over its main diagonal. Second, reverse each row. Iterate `i` from 0 to `n`. Reverse the row `matrix[i]` using a two-pointer approach (or `matrix[i].reverse()`).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def rotate(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
n = len(matrix)
# 1. Transpose the matrix
for i in range(n):
for j in range(i, n):
matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]
# 2. Reverse each row
for i in range(n):
matrix[i].reverse()

data.title: Set All Elements in Matrix Zeroes In-Place
data.description: Given an `m x n` matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. You must do this in-place. A naive solution using O(m*n) space is easy. An O(m+n) space solution is also simple. The optimal O(1) space solution is tricky. It uses the *first row* and *first column* of the matrix itself as storage to mark which rows/cols need to be zeroed.
data.short_answer: Use O(1) space. Use `is_first_col_zero` as a flag. Iterate through the matrix. If `matrix[i][j] == 0`, set `matrix[i][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][j] = 0` (or set the flag if `j=0`). Now, iterate from `i=1, j=1`. If `matrix[i][0] == 0` or `matrix[0][j] == 0`, set `matrix[i][j] = 0`. Finally, zero out the first row and first column if needed (based on their original 0s).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def setZeroes(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
ROWS, COLS = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
is_first_col_zero = False
for r in range(ROWS):
if matrix[r][0] == 0:
is_first_col_zero = True
for c in range(1, COLS):
if matrix[r][c] == 0:
matrix[r][0] = 0
matrix[0][c] = 0
for r in range(ROWS - 1, -1, -1):
for c in range(COLS - 1, 0, -1):
if matrix[r][0] == 0 or matrix[0][c] == 0:
matrix[r][c] = 0
if is_first_col_zero:
matrix[r][0] = 0

data.title: Traverse a Matrix in Spiral Order
data.description: Given an `m x n` matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order. For example, a 3x3 matrix `[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]` should return `[1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5]`. This is a classic simulation problem that tests your ability to manage boundaries. You need to simulate the traversal by 'peeling' the outer layer of the matrix.
data.short_answer: Use four pointers to track the boundaries: `top = 0`, `bottom = m-1`, `left = 0`, `right = n-1`. Use a loop `while left <= right and top <= bottom`. In the loop: 1) Traverse Right: from `left` to `right` at row `top`. 2) Traverse Down: from `top+1` to `bottom` at col `right`. 3) Traverse Left: from `right-1` to `left`. 4) Traverse Up: from `bottom-1` to `top+1`. After each traversal, shrink the corresponding boundary.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def spiralOrder(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
if not matrix: return []
ROWS, COLS = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
top, bottom = 0, ROWS - 1
left, right = 0, COLS - 1
result = []
while left <= right and top <= bottom:
for c in range(left, right + 1):
result.append(matrix[top][c])
top += 1
for r in range(top, bottom + 1):
result.append(matrix[r][right])
right -= 1
if not (left <= right and top <= bottom):
break
for c in range(right, left - 1, -1):
result.append(matrix[bottom][c])
bottom -= 1
for r in range(bottom, top - 1, -1):
result.append(matrix[r][left])
left += 1
return result

data.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals in an Array
data.description: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals. For example, `[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]]` becomes `[[1,6],[8,10]]`. This is a very common problem that tests sorting and greedy logic. The key is to sort by the start time.
data.short_answer: First, sort the `intervals` array based on the `start` time. Create a `result` list and add the first interval. Now, iterate through the rest of the intervals. Let the last interval in `result` be `last_interval`. If the current `interval.start` is *less than or equal to* `last_interval.end`, they overlap. Merge them by updating `last_interval.end = max(last_interval.end, interval.end)`. If they don't overlap, add the current `interval` to `result`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def merge(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
if not intervals: return []
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
result = [intervals[0]]
for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
last_interval = result[-1]
curr_interval = intervals[i]
if curr_interval[0] <= last_interval[1]:
last_interval[1] = max(last_interval[1], curr_interval[1])
else:
result.append(curr_interval)
return result

data.title: Find the Kth Largest Element in an Array
data.description: Given an integer array `nums` and `k`, return the `k`th largest element. This is a classic selection problem. The O(n log n) solution is to sort. The O(n log k) solution is to use a min-heap of size `k`. The optimal O(n) average-case solution is **Quickselect**, which is a modification of Quicksort.
data.short_answer: Use a Min-Heap of size `k`. Iterate through `nums`. For each `num`, push it onto the heap. If `len(heap) > k`, pop the smallest element. This ensures the heap always contains the `k` largest elements. After the loop, the root of the heap (`heap[0]`) is the `k`-th largest. (The Quickselect solution is also a valid and often preferred answer).
data.tags: Array, Sorting, Heap, Priority Queue, Quickselect
data.python_code:
import heapq
class Solution:
def findKthLargest(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
min_heap = []
for num in nums:
heapq.heappush(min_heap, num)
if len(min_heap) > k:
heapq.heappop(min_heap)
return min_heap[0]

data.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array (O(1) Space)
data.description: Given an array `nums` of `n` integers where `nums[i]` is in `[1, n]`, return an array of all integers in `[1, n]` that do *not* appear in `nums`. You must solve this in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (excluding the output). This is another 'in-place hash' problem, similar to 'Find All Duplicates'. We use the array's indices and the sign of the numbers to mark which are seen.
data.short_answer: Use the in-place marking method. Iterate through `nums`. For each `num`, get its value `x = abs(num)`. The index it corresponds to is `idx = x - 1`. 'Mark' this index as seen by flipping the sign of the number at that index: `nums[idx] = -abs(nums[idx])`. After this first pass, iterate from `i = 0` to `n-1`. If `nums[i]` is *positive*, it means the index `i` was never marked. Thus, the number `i + 1` is missing.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def findDisappearedNumbers(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
for num in nums:
idx = abs(num) - 1
nums[idx] = -abs(nums[idx])
result = []
for i in range(len(nums)):
if nums[i] > 0:
result.append(i + 1)
return result

data.title: Find the Subarray Sum That Equals K
data.description: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `k`, find the total number of continuous subarrays whose sum equals `k`. This is a very common and important problem. A naive O(n^2) solution (checking all subarrays) will time out. The optimal O(n) solution uses a hash map to store the frequencies of *prefix sums*.
data.short_answer: Use a hash map `prefix_sums` to store `sum -> frequency`. Initialize `prefix_sums[0] = 1`. Maintain a `current_sum = 0` and `count = 0`. Iterate through `nums`. Add `num` to `current_sum`. We are looking for a previous sum `prev_sum` such that `current_sum - prev_sum = k`. This is `prev_sum = current_sum - k`. Check if `prev_sum` is in the map. If it is, `count += prefix_sums[prev_sum]`. Finally, increment `prefix_sums[current_sum]`.
data.python_code:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
def subarraySum(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
prefix_sums = defaultdict(int)
prefix_sums[0] = 1
current_sum = 0
count = 0
for num in nums:
current_sum += num
complement = current_sum - k
count += prefix_sums[complement]
prefix_sums[current_sum] += 1
return count

data.title: Generate the Next Lexicographical Permutation
data.description: Given an array of integers `nums`, find the next lexicographically greater permutation. If no such permutation exists, rearrange it to the lowest (sorted ascending). This must be in-place with O(1) space. This is a classic algorithm problem. It requires finding the first 'dip' from the right, swapping it, and then reversing the rest.
data.short_answer: 1. Find the first 'dip': iterate from `i = n-2` backwards. Stop at the first `i` where `nums[i] < nums[i+1]`. 2. If no such `i` exists, the array is sorted descending. Reverse it and return. 3. Find the 'ceiling': iterate from `j = n-1` backwards to `i`. Find the first `j` where `nums[j] > nums[i]`. 4. Swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`. 5. Reverse the *suffix* of the array starting from `i + 1`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def nextPermutation(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
n = len(nums)
i = n - 2
while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i + 1]:
i -= 1
if i == -1:
nums.reverse()
return
j = n - 1
while nums[j] <= nums[i]:
j -= 1
nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
nums[i+1:] = nums[i+1:][::-1]

data.title: Determine if You Can Jump to the End of an Array
data.description: You are given an array `nums` where `nums[i]` is the maximum jump length from that position. You start at index 0. Return `true` if you can reach the last index. This is a classic 'greedy' array problem. We don't need to know *how* we get to the end, just *if* we can. We can track the 'farthest' reachable index.
data.short_answer: Use a greedy approach. Maintain a variable `max_reach` (initialized to 0). Iterate through the array with `i`. At each `i`, check if `i > max_reach`. If it is, it means we fell short and can never reach `i`. Return `false`. Otherwise, update `max_reach = max(max_reach, i + nums[i])`. If `max_reach` ever becomes `>= n - 1`, we can reach the end, so return `true`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def canJump(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
max_reach = 0
n = len(nums)
for i in range(n):
if i > max_reach:
return False
max_reach = max(max_reach, i + nums[i])
if max_reach >= n - 1:
return True
return True

data.title: Find Minimum Jumps to Reach End of Array (Jump Game II)
data.description: Given an array `nums` where `nums[i]` is the max jump length, find the *minimum* number of jumps to reach the last index. This is the follow-up to 'Jump Game' and is also a greedy problem. This is a common and clever O(n) solution that is a form of Breadth-First Search.
data.short_answer: Use a greedy BFS approach. Maintain `jumps = 0`, `current_farthest` (the end of the current 'level'), and `next_farthest` (the max reach from *within* the current level). Iterate from `i = 0` to `n-1`. Update `next_farthest = max(next_farthest, i + nums[i])`. When `i == current_farthest` (you've reached the end of the current 'jump'), increment `jumps` and set `current_farthest = next_farthest`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def jump(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
jumps = 0
current_farthest = 0
next_farthest = 0
n = len(nums)
for i in range(n - 1):
next_farthest = max(next_farthest, i + nums[i])
if i == current_farthest:
jumps += 1
current_farthest = next_farthest
return jumps

data.title: Find the Majority Element in an Array (Boyer-Moore)
data.description: Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the majority element. The majority element is the element that appears more than `floor(n / 2)` times. You may assume one always exists. The hash map solution is O(n) time and O(n) space. The optimal O(n) time, O(1) space solution is the **Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm**.
data.short_answer: Use the Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm. Initialize `count = 0` and `candidate = None`. Iterate through `nums`. If `count == 0`, set `candidate = num`. Then, if `num == candidate`, increment `count`. If `num != candidate`, decrement `count`. The `candidate` remaining at the end will be the majority element.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, Sorting, Boyer-Moore Voting
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def majorityElement(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
count = 0
candidate = None
for num in nums:
if count == 0:
candidate = num
count += (1 if num == candidate else -1)
return candidate

data.title: Find All Majority Elements II (More than n/3)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums` of size `n`, find all elements that appear more than `floor(n / 3)` times. This is a follow-up to the 'Majority Element' problem. At most, there can be *two* such elements. This is solved with a modified Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm that tracks two candidates and two counters.
data.short_answer: Use a modified Boyer-Moore. Maintain two candidates and two counters (`c1`, `c2`, `v1`, `v2`). Iterate: if `num == v1`, `c1++`. If `num == v2`, `c2++`. If `c1 == 0`, `v1 = num, c1 = 1`. If `c2 == 0`, `v2 = num, c2 = 1`. Else, `c1--` and `c2--`. After this first pass, you have two *potential* candidates. You must perform a *second pass* to count their actual frequencies and verify if they are `> n / 3`.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, Sorting, Boyer-Moore Voting
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def majorityElement(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
if not nums: return []
v1, v2, c1, c2 = None, None, 0, 0
for num in nums:
if num == v1:
c1 += 1
elif num == v2:
c2 += 1
elif c1 == 0:
v1, c1 = num, 1
elif c2 == 0:
v2, c2 = num, 1
else:
c1 -= 1
c2 -= 1
result = []
for v in [v1, v2]:
if nums.count(v) > len(nums) // 3:
result.append(v)
return list(set(result))

data.title: Insert a New Interval into a Sorted List of Intervals
data.description: You are given a list of non-overlapping, sorted `intervals` and a `newInterval`. Insert `newInterval` such that the list remains sorted and non-overlapping (merging if necessary). This is a common interval problem. It's a variation of 'Merge Intervals' but with a list that is already sorted, so we can do it in a single pass.
data.short_answer: Create a `result` list. Iterate through `intervals`. 1. Add all intervals that end *before* `newInterval` starts (`interval.end < newInterval.start`). 2. Once you find an overlap (or the insertion point), start merging. While `interval.start <= newInterval.end`, merge them by updating `newInterval = [min(newInterval.start, interval.start), max(newInterval.end, interval.end)]`. 3. After merging, add the `newInterval`. 4. Add all remaining intervals.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
result = []
i = 0
n = len(intervals)
# 1. Add all intervals before newInterval
while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
result.append(intervals[i])
i += 1
# 2. Merge overlapping intervals
while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
i += 1
result.append(newInterval)
# 3. Add remaining intervals
while i < n:
result.append(intervals[i])
i += 1
return result

data.title: Generate All Subsets (The Power Set)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. This is a fundamental backtracking problem. The core idea is to make a decision for each element: either 'include' it in the current subset or 'exclude' it. This binary choice (include/exclude) for `n` elements naturally leads to 2^n possible subsets.
data.short_answer: Use a recursive backtracking function, `dfs(start, path)`. `start` is the index to begin choosing from, `path` is the current subset. First, add a *copy* of `path` to the `result`. Then, iterate `i` from `start` to `n-1`. 'Choose' `nums[i]` (add to `path`), make a recursive call `dfs(i + 1, path)`, and then 'unchoose' `nums[i]` (pop from `path`).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def subsets(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
result = []
path = []
def backtrack(start_index):
result.append(path[:])
for i in range(start_index, len(nums)):
path.append(nums[i])
backtrack(i + 1)
path.pop()
backtrack(0)
return result

data.title: Generate All Combinations that Sum to a Target
data.description: Given an array of distinct integers `candidates` and a `target`, return a list of all unique combinations of `candidates` where the numbers sum to `target`. The *same* number may be chosen an unlimited number of times. This is another classic backtracking problem where the 'state' includes the remaining sum needed.
data.short_answer: Use a backtracking function `dfs(start, remaining_target, path)`. The base cases: if `remaining_target == 0`, add a copy of `path` to the result. If `remaining_target < 0`, return. In the loop (from `i = start` to `n-1`), 'choose' `candidates[i]`: add it to `path` and make a recursive call `dfs(i, remaining_target - candidates[i], path)`. Note: we pass `i`, not `i+1`, to allow reuse. Then, 'unchoose' (pop from `path`).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def combinationSum(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
result = []
path = []
def backtrack(start_index, remaining_target):
if remaining_target == 0:
result.append(path[:])
return
if remaining_target < 0:
return

for i in range(start_index, len(candidates)):
path.append(candidates[i])
backtrack(i, remaining_target - candidates[i])
path.pop()

backtrack(0, target)
return result

data.title: Generate All Combinations of Size K from N Numbers
data.description: Given two integers `n` and `k`, return all possible combinations of `k` numbers chosen from the range `[1, n]`. This is a classic backtracking problem where we explore the decision of either 'including' a number in our combination or skipping it. Unlike permutations, the order does not matter (so `[1,2]` is the same as `[2,1]`), which we handle by only choosing numbers in increasing order.
data.short_answer: Use a recursive backtracking function `dfs(start, path)`. The `start` parameter ensures we only pick numbers greater than the previous one, avoiding duplicate combinations. The base case is when `len(path) == k`, at which point we add a copy of `path` to the result. In the loop, iterate `i` from `start` to `n`. 'Choose' `i`, recurse `dfs(i + 1, path)`, and then 'unchoose' (pop).
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def combine(self, n: int, k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
result = []
path = []
def backtrack(start_num):
if len(path) == k:
result.append(path[:])
return
for i in range(start_num, n + 1):
path.append(i)
backtrack(i + 1)
path.pop()
backtrack(1)
return result

data.title: Find the Missing Number in an Array from 1 to N
data.description: Given an array `nums` containing `n` distinct numbers in the range `[0, n]`, return the *only* number in the range that is missing from the array. This is a classic problem with several solutions. A hash set works (O(n) space). The optimal O(1) space solution uses the 'Cyclic Sort' pattern (placing numbers at their correct index) or a mathematical approach using Gauss's formula for the expected sum.
data.short_answer: The optimal solution uses Gauss's formula. Calculate the expected sum of all numbers from 0 to `n`: `expected_sum = n * (n + 1) // 2`. Calculate the `actual_sum` of the `nums` array. The missing number is simply the difference: `expected_sum - actual_sum`. This is an O(n) time, O(1) space solution.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, Math, Bit Manipulation, Cyclic Sort
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def missingNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
n = len(nums)
expected_sum = n * (n + 1) // 2
actual_sum = sum(nums)
return expected_sum - actual_sum

data.title: Increment a Large Integer Represented as an Array
data.description: You are given a large integer represented as an array `digits`, where `digits[i]` is the `i`-th digit (most significant first). Increment the integer by one. For `[1,2,3]`, return `[1,2,4]`. The challenge is handling the 'carry', especially in cases like `[9,9,9]`, which must become `[1,0,0,0]`. This problem tests basic arithmetic and array manipulation.
data.short_answer: Iterate through the `digits` array from *right to left* (`i = n-1` down to 0). At each position, add 1: `digits[i] += 1`. If the digit is now less than 10 (e.g., 4 -> 5), we are done. Return `digits`. If the digit becomes 10, set `digits[i] = 0` and continue the loop (to 'carry' the 1). If the loop finishes and the first digit is 0 (e.g., [9,9] -> [0,0]), it means we have an overflow. Insert a 1 at the beginning.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def plusOne(self, digits: list[int]) -> list[int]:
n = len(digits)
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
if digits[i] < 9:
digits[i] += 1
return digits
digits[i] = 0

# If we're here, all digits were 9
return [1] + digits

data.title: Find the Single Number (Appears Once, Others Twice)
data.description: Given a non-empty array of integers `nums`, every element appears *twice* except for one. Find that single one. This is a classic bit manipulation problem. The key is to use the XOR operation (`^`). The XOR of a number with itself is 0 (`a ^ a = 0`). The XOR of a number with 0 is itself (`a ^ 0 = a`). All pairs will cancel out.
data.short_answer: Initialize `result = 0`. Iterate through the `nums` array. For each `num`, XOR it with the `result`: `result = result ^ num`. All the numbers that appear twice will cancel each other out (e.g., `a ^ b ^ a = b`). The only number remaining in `result` will be the one that appeared once. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def singleNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
result = 0
for num in nums:
result ^= num
return result

data.title: Find the Pivot Index (Equilibrium Point)
data.description: Given an array of integers `nums`, find the 'pivot index'. This is the index where the sum of all numbers to the *left* of the index is equal to the sum of all numbers to the *right*. If no such index exists, return -1. This is a classic prefix sum problem. A naive O(n^2) solution (re-calculating sums) is too slow. The O(n) solution involves one pass to get the total sum, and a second to check the condition.
data.short_answer: First, calculate the `total_sum` of the entire array. Initialize `left_sum = 0`. Iterate through the array with `i`. In the loop, calculate `right_sum = total_sum - left_sum - nums[i]`. Check if `left_sum == right_sum`. If they are equal, return `i`. If not, update `left_sum += nums[i]` and continue. If the loop finishes, return -1.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def pivotIndex(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
total_sum = sum(nums)
left_sum = 0
for i in range(len(nums)):
right_sum = total_sum - left_sum - nums[i]
if left_sum == right_sum:
return i
left_sum += nums[i]
return -1

data.title: Calculate the Range Sum Query (Immutable)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, handle multiple queries of this type: Calculate the sum of elements of `nums` between indices `left` and `right` inclusive. This is a classic problem to introduce **Prefix Sums**. A naive solution would re-calculate the sum for each query (O(n) per query). By pre-calculating a prefix sum array, we can answer each query in O(1) time.
data.short_answer: Create a `prefix_sum` array of size `n+1`, initialized to 0. Iterate through `nums`, and calculate `prefix_sum[i+1] = prefix_sum[i] + nums[i]`. This pre-computation takes O(n) time. Now, for any query `(left, right)`, the sum is `prefix_sum[right + 1] - prefix_sum[left]`. This is an O(1) operation.
data.python_code:
class NumArray:
def __init__(self, nums: list[int]):
self.prefix_sum = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)
for i in range(len(nums)):
self.prefix_sum[i + 1] = self.prefix_sum[i] + nums[i]

def sumRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> int:
return self.prefix_sum[right + 1] - self.prefix_sum[left]

data.title: Find the K-th Largest Element in an Array (Quickselect)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums` and `k`, return the `k`th largest element. This is a classic selection problem. The optimal O(n) *average* case solution is **Quickselect**, which is a modification of Quicksort. We partition the array around a pivot, but unlike Quicksort, we only recurse on the *one* side that contains our target index.
data.short_answer: Use a recursive function `quickSelect(left, right, k_smallest)`. Note: `k_smallest` is `n - k`. Choose a pivot (e.g., `pivot = nums[right]`). Partition the array around the pivot. Let the pivot's final index be `pivot_index`. If `pivot_index == k_smallest`, we found it. If `pivot_index < k_smallest`, recurse on the right. If `pivot_index > k_smallest`, recurse on the left.
data.tags: Array, Sorting, Quickselect, Divide and Conquer
data.python_code:
import random
class Solution:
def findKthLargest(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
k_smallest_idx = len(nums) - k

def partition(left, right):
pivot_val = nums[right]
store_idx = left
for i in range(left, right):
if nums[i] <= pivot_val:
nums[store_idx], nums[i] = nums[i], nums[store_idx]
store_idx += 1
nums[right], nums[store_idx] = nums[store_idx], nums[right]
return store_idx

def quickSelect(left, right):
if left == right:
return nums[left]
pivot_idx = partition(left, right)
if pivot_idx == k_smallest_idx:
return nums[pivot_idx]
elif pivot_idx < k_smallest_idx:
return quickSelect(pivot_idx + 1, right)
else:
return quickSelect(left, pivot_idx - 1)

return quickSelect(0, len(nums) - 1)

data.title: Sort an Array of Squares of a Sorted Array
data.description: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted. A naive solution (square all, then sort) is O(n log n). The optimal O(n) solution uses a **two-pointer** approach, because the original array is sorted. The largest squared values will be at the *ends* of the original array.
data.short_answer: Use two pointers, `left = 0` and `right = n - 1`. Create a `result` array of size `n`. Use a third pointer `p_write` starting at `n - 1` (to fill `result` from the back). While `left <= right`: compare the absolute values `abs(nums[left])` and `abs(nums[right])`. Place the square of the larger one at `result[p_write]`. Move the corresponding pointer (`left` or `right`) inward, and move `p_write` inward.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def sortedSquares(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
n = len(nums)
result = [0] * n
left, right = 0, n - 1
p_write = n - 1
while left <= right:
if abs(nums[left]) > abs(nums[right]):
result[p_write] = nums[left] * nums[left]
left += 1
else:
result[p_write] = nums[right] * nums[right]
right -= 1
p_write -= 1
return result

data.title: Find the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
data.description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (LIS). A subsequence can be non-contiguous. For `[10,9,2,5,3,7]`, the LIS is `[2,3,7]` (length 3). The classic DP solution is O(n^2). An optimal O(n log n) solution exists that uses an auxiliary array and Binary Search.
data.short_answer: The O(n log n) solution uses a 'patience sorting' or 'tails' array, `sub`. Iterate through `nums`. For each `num`: if `sub` is empty or `num > sub[-1]`, it extends the LIS, so append `num` to `sub`. If `num` is *not* greater, it means `num` can be a *better* (smaller) end for a subsequence of some length. Use Binary Search (`bisect_left`) on `sub` to find the first element `sub[i]` that is `>= num`. Replace `sub[i]` with `num`. The final `len(sub)` is the answer.
data.tags: Array, Dynamic Programming, DP, Binary Search, LIS
data.python_code:
import bisect
class Solution:
def lengthOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
sub = []
for num in nums:
if not sub or num > sub[-1]:
sub.append(num)
else:
idx = bisect.bisect_left(sub, num)
sub[idx] = num
return len(sub)

data.title: Implement the Coin Change Problem (Minimum Coins)
data.description: You are given an array of `coins` of different denominations and a total `amount`. Find the minimum number of coins that you need to make up that amount. If it cannot be made up, return -1. This is a classic 'unbounded knapsack' dynamic programming problem. We want to find the minimum for each sub-amount up to the target.
data.short_answer: Use a 1D DP array, `dp`, of size `amount + 1`, initialized to `float('inf')`. `dp[i]` is the min coins for amount `i`. Set `dp[0] = 0`. Iterate `i` from 1 to `amount`. For each `i`, iterate through the `coins`. If `coin <= i`, then `dp[i] = min(dp[i], 1 + dp[i - coin])`. This checks if using this `coin` provides a better solution. The answer is `dp[amount]`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def coinChange(self, coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
dp = [float('inf')] * (amount + 1)
dp[0] = 0

for i in range(1, amount + 1):
for coin in coins:
if i - coin >= 0:
dp[i] = min(dp[i], 1 + dp[i - coin])

return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1

data.title: Find the Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling (DP + Binary Search)
data.description: You have `n` jobs. You are given `startTime`, `endTime`, and `profit` arrays. Find the maximum profit you can take such that there are no overlapping jobs. This is a hard DP problem. `dp[i]` = max profit from job `i` onwards. The key is that after doing job `i`, you must find the *next non-overlapping* job. This search can be optimized from O(n) to O(log n) using Binary Search.
data.short_answer: Sort the jobs by `startTime`. Create a recursive `dp(i)` with memoization. `dp(i)` is the max profit from `jobs[i:]`. We have two choices: 1. Skip job `i`: profit is `dp(i+1)`. 2. Take job `i`: profit is `jobs[i].profit + dp(next_job_index)`. To find `next_job_index`, use Binary Search ('lower bound') on the `startTime` array to find the first job `j` where `startTime[j] >= endTime[i]`. Return `max(choice1, choice2)`.
data.tags: Array, Sorting, Dynamic Programming, DP, Binary Search
data.python_code:
import bisect
class Solution:
def jobScheduling(self, startTime: list[int], endTime: list[int], profit: list[int]) -> int:
jobs = sorted(zip(startTime, endTime, profit))
n = len(jobs)
memo = {}
sorted_start_times = [job[0] for job in jobs]

def dp(i):
if i == n: return 0
if i in memo: return memo[i]

profit_skip = dp(i + 1)

current_end_time = jobs[i][1]
next_job_index = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_start_times, current_end_time)
profit_take = jobs[i][2] + dp(next_job_index)

memo[i] = max(profit_skip, profit_take)
return memo[i]

return dp(0)

data.title: Find the Longest Subarray with Sum Divisible by K
data.description: Given an array `nums` and `k`, find the length of the longest subarray whose sum is divisible by `k`. This is a classic 'Prefix Sum' problem combined with a hash map. The key insight is that if `(prefix_sum[j] % k) == (prefix_sum[i] % k)`, then the sum of the subarray `nums[i+1...j]` must be divisible by `k`.
data.short_answer: Use a hash map `remainder_map` to store `remainder -> first_index`. Initialize `map[0] = -1`. Maintain a `current_sum = 0` and `max_len = 0`. Iterate through `nums` with index `i`. Add `nums[i]` to `current_sum`. Calculate `remainder = current_sum % k`. If `remainder` is *in* the map, it means a subarray ends here: `max_len = max(max_len, i - map[remainder])`. If `remainder` is *not* in the map, add it: `map[remainder] = i`.
data.tags: Array, Hash Table, Prefix Sum, Modulo
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def longSubarrWthSumDivByK(self, arr, n, k):
remainder_map = {0: -1}
current_sum = 0
max_len = 0
for i in range(n):
current_sum += arr[i]
remainder = current_sum % k
if remainder < 0:
remainder += k

if remainder in remainder_map:
max_len = max(max_len, i - remainder_map[remainder])
else:
remainder_map[remainder] = i
return max_len

data.title: Find the Median of a Row-wise Sorted Matrix
data.description: Given an `m x n` matrix where each row is sorted, find the overall median of the matrix. Assume `m * n` is odd. This is a classic 'Binary Search on the Answer' problem. The median is the element that has `(m*n) / 2` elements smaller than it. We can binary search for the *value* of the median in the range of possible values (min to max in the matrix).
data.short_answer: Find the `min_val` and `max_val` in the matrix (e.g., `mat[0][0]` and `mat[n-1][m-1]` range). This is the search space. Binary search for `mid_val`. For each `mid_val`, count how many elements in the *entire matrix* are `<= mid_val`. This count can be found in O(m log n) by using Binary Search ('upper bound') on each row. Let this be `count`. If `count <= (m*n) // 2`, the median is larger (`left = mid + 1`). If `count > (m*n) // 2`, `mid_val` is a possible median (`right = mid - 1`).
data.tags: Array, Matrix, Binary Search, Binary Search on Answer
data.python_code:
import bisect
class Solution:
def median(self, matrix, r, c):
min_val = min(row[0] for row in matrix)
max_val = max(row[-1] for row in matrix)
target_count = (r * c) // 2
ans = max_val

while min_val <= max_val:
mid_val = (min_val + max_val) // 2
count = 0
for row in matrix:
count += bisect.bisect_right(row, mid_val)

if count <= target_count:
min_val = mid_val + 1
else:
ans = mid_val
max_val = mid_val - 1
return ans

data.title: Generate Pascal's Triangle up to N Rows
data.description: Given an integer `numRows`, generate the first `numRows` of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it. This is a straightforward DP or simulation problem. Each new row can be built from the previous row.
data.short_answer: Initialize `triangle = [[1]]`. Loop from `i = 1` to `numRows - 1`. Get the `prev_row`. Create a `new_row` starting with `[1]`. Iterate `j` from 1 to `len(prev_row) - 1`. The value is `prev_row[j-1] + prev_row[j]`. Append this to `new_row`. After the inner loop, append `1` to `new_row`. Append `new_row` to `triangle`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def generate(self, numRows: int) -> list[list[int]]:
if numRows == 0: return []
triangle = [[1]]
for i in range(1, numRows):
prev_row = triangle[-1]
new_row = [1]
for j in range(len(prev_row) - 1):
new_row.append(prev_row[j] + prev_row[j+1])
new_row.append(1)
triangle.append(new_row)
return triangle

data.title: Find the K-th Row of Pascal's Triangle (O(k) Space)
data.description: Given an integer `rowIndex`, return the `rowIndex`-th (0-indexed) row of Pascal's triangle. This is a follow-up to the previous problem. The challenge is to do this with only O(k) extra space, where `k` is the `rowIndex`. This means we can't store the whole triangle. We must compute the row iteratively, modifying a single list in place.
data.short_answer: The O(k) space solution involves clever in-place updates. Start with `row = [1]`. Loop `i` from 1 to `rowIndex`. In the loop, iterate `j` from `i-1` *down to* 1. Update `row[j] = row[j] + row[j-1]`. This 'back-to-front' update is crucial to avoid using the *new* value in the same pass. After the inner loop, append a `1` to the end.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def getRow(self, rowIndex: int) -> list[int]:
row = [1]
for i in range(rowIndex):
for j in range(len(row) - 1, 0, -1):
row[j] = row[j] + row[j-1]
row.append(1)
return row

data.title: Find the Longest Subarray of 1s After Deleting One Element
data.description: Given a binary array `nums`, you must delete *exactly one* element. Return the size of the longest subarray of `1`s in the resulting array. If there is no such subarray, return 0. This is a sliding window problem. We are looking for the longest window that contains at most *one* zero.
data.short_answer: Use a sliding window. Maintain `zero_count = 0` and `max_len = 0`. Use a `left` pointer. Iterate `right` through `nums`. If `nums[right] == 0`, increment `zero_count`. While `zero_count > 1`, the window is invalid. Shrink it by incrementing `left` and decrementing `zero_count` if `nums[left] == 0`. The length of the valid window is `right - left`. Update `max_len = max(max_len, right - left)`. The final answer is `max_len`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def longestSubarray(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
left = 0
zero_count = 0
max_len = 0
for right in range(len(nums)):
if nums[right] == 0:
zero_count += 1
while zero_count > 1:
if nums[left] == 0:
zero_count -= 1
left += 1
max_len = max(max_len, right - left)
return max_len

data.title: Find the Maximum Number of Consecutive Ones
data.description: Given a binary array `nums`, return the maximum number of consecutive `1`s in the array. This is a simple one-pass traversal problem. We just need to keep track of the current 'streak' of 1s and update a global maximum.
data.short_answer: Initialize `max_consecutive = 0` and `current_consecutive = 0`. Iterate through the `nums` array. If `num == 1`, increment `current_consecutive`. If `num == 0`, it means the streak is broken. Update `max_consecutive = max(max_consecutive, current_consecutive)` and reset `current_consecutive = 0`. After the loop, do one final check of `max_consecutive` against `current_consecutive`.
data.python_code:
class Solution:
def findMaxConsecutiveOnes(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
max_consecutive = 0
current_consecutive = 0
for num in nums:
if num == 1:
current_consecutive += 1
else:
max_consecutive = max(max_consecutive, current_consecutive)
current_consecutive = 0
return max(max_consecutive, current_consecutive)

data.title: Find Maximum Consecutive Ones III (K Flips)
data.description: Given a binary array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum number of consecutive `1`s in the array if you can flip at most `k` `0`s to `1`s.
